units.title: People and the verb sein
units.summary: Use ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir sind, ihr seid, and sie/Sie sind. Capital Sie means formal you.

units.title: Present tense and personal endings
units.summary: Regular verbs usually take -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en. The verb is normally the second element in a statement.

units.title: Questions and verb position
units.summary: A yes/no question starts with the conjugated verb. A question word such as wo or wann comes first, followed by the verb.

units.title: Noun gender, articles and plurals
units.summary: Learn a noun with its article and plural. Der, die and das mark grammatical gender. All plural nouns use die in the nominative.

units.title: Things you buy and need
units.summary: A direct object takes the accusative. Masculine der/ein become den/einen; die/eine and das/ein stay the same.

units.title: Saying no: nicht and kein
units.summary: Use kein to negate a noun with no article or an indefinite article. Use nicht to negate a verb, adjective or a specific statement.

units.title: Belonging: mein, dein and ihr
units.summary: A possessive determiner agrees with the noun: mein Bruder, meine Schwester, mein Buch. Ihr can mean her or their; Ihr with a capital letter means your (formal).

units.title: Can, must and would like
units.summary: A modal verb is conjugated in second position. The other verb stays in the infinitive at the end: ich kann helfen; wir müssen gehen. Möchte expresses would like.

units.title: Verbs with a detachable beginning
units.summary: In a simple main clause, a separable prefix moves to the end: anfangen → der Film fängt an. With a modal, the infinitive stays together.

units.title: Times, dates and routine
units.summary: Use um for clock times, am for days or dates, and im for months or seasons: um acht, am Montag, im Oktober.

units.title: With me, for you: frequent prepositions
units.summary: Mit, bei, von, zu, aus and nach take the dative. Learn common chunks first: mit dem Bus, bei meiner Freundin, zum Bahnhof. Zu dem contracts to zum; zu der to zur.

units.title: Polite requests and everyday instructions
units.summary: Bitte softens a request. For a formal instruction, use the verb followed by Sie: Warten Sie bitte. A simple informal imperative can omit the subject.

units.title: Telling what happened: the perfect
units.summary: Most conversational past events use haben/sein + past participle. The auxiliary is conjugated; the participle goes at the end. Movement to a destination often uses sein.

units.title: Useful simple past: war and hatte
units.summary: Sein and haben often use the simple past in conversation: ich war, du warst, wir waren; ich hatte, du hattest, wir hatten.

units.title: Reasons with weil and dass
units.summary: Weil introduces a reason; dass introduces a reported statement. In these subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb goes at the end.

units.title: If and when: wenn
units.summary: Wenn describes a condition, a repeated event, or a future time. Put the verb last in the wenn clause. If that clause comes first, the main clause starts with its verb.

units.title: Comparing and choosing
units.summary: Use adjective + -er and als to compare: kleiner als. Some forms change: gut → besser, viel → mehr. Am ...-sten expresses the highest degree.

units.title: Where something is and where it goes
units.summary: An, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor and zwischen take the dative for location and the accusative for a destination. Ask wo? for location and wohin? for destination.

units.title: Replacing things and people
units.summary: Accusative pronouns include mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch. Dative pronouns include mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen. The verb determines the case: sehen + accusative; helfen + dative.

units.title: Describing a particular thing
units.summary: An adjective before a noun needs an ending. After a definite article in the nominative, a singular adjective usually ends in -e: der alte Bahnhof, die kleine Tasche, das neue Buch.

units.title: Actions that return to the subject
units.summary: Some verbs need a reflexive pronoun: sich freuen, sich erinnern, sich treffen. Use ich ... mich, du ... dich, and er/sie ... sich. Learn associated prepositions as chunks.

units.title: Plans with zu and purpose with um ... zu
units.summary: After many verbs and expressions, use zu + infinitive: versuchen zu helfen. Um ... zu states a purpose when both actions have the same subject.

units.title: Polite possibilities with könnte and würde
units.summary: Könnte makes a request less direct. Würde + infinitive can express a wish or hypothetical action. Hätte gern is a polite way to ask for something.

units.title: Joining plans with deshalb and trotzdem
units.summary: Deshalb means therefore and links a reason to its result. Trotzdem means nevertheless. They occupy first position when placed at the start, so the conjugated verb follows.

units.title: Identifying people with relative clauses
units.summary: A relative clause gives extra information about a noun. Its relative pronoun reflects gender/number and its role inside the clause. The conjugated verb goes last.

units.title: Reporting processes with the passive
units.summary: Use werden + past participle for an action focused on what happens, rather than who does it. A present passive is wird repariert; a past passive can be wurde repariert.

units.title: Reading stories in the simple past
units.summary: Written narratives often use the Präteritum: ging, sah, fand, nahm, sagte. Strong verbs can change their vowel; weak verbs usually add -te.

units.title: What had already happened
units.summary: Use the past perfect for an event before another past event: hatte/war + past participle. Make the earlier/later relationship explicit with schon, bevor or nachdem.

units.title: Although and nevertheless
units.summary: Obwohl introduces a subordinate clause with the verb last. Trotzdem joins a separate main clause with normal second-position verb order.

units.title: Explaining who benefits: damit
units.summary: Use damit for a purpose, especially when the two clauses have different subjects. The verb goes last in the damit clause. Um ... zu usually requires the same subject.

units.title: Reporting questions without asking directly
units.summary: An indirect yes/no question starts with ob. An indirect question with wo, wann or warum keeps that word. In both cases the conjugated verb goes last.

units.title: Imagining a different situation
units.summary: For hypothetical situations, use wenn + Konjunktiv II forms such as hätte, wäre, könnte or würde + infinitive. They also let you give tactful advice.

units.title: Verbs with a fixed preposition
units.summary: Learn verb, preposition and case as one chunk: warten auf + accusative, teilnehmen an + dative, sich interessieren für + accusative. Da-/wo- compounds usually refer to things.

units.title: During, since and until
units.summary: Seit + dative describes a state that began in the past and continues now. Während + genitive describes a duration. Bis indicates an endpoint and often appears with another preposition.

units.title: Formal written relationships: the genitive
units.summary: The genitive can express belonging: der Name des Dorfes, die Entscheidung der Frau. Masculine/neuter nouns often add -(e)s. This is common in notices and formal writing.

units.title: Organizing a balanced argument
units.summary: Einerseits ... andererseits presents two sides. Zwar ... aber recognizes a point then limits it. Use specific reasons and an explicit conclusion rather than merely adding connectors.

examples.english: It is raining. Therefore I take the bus.

examples.german: Ich bin müde. Trotzdem komme ich mit.
examples.english: I am tired. Nevertheless I am coming along.

grammar.title: Identifying people with relative clauses
grammar.explanation: A relative clause gives extra information about a noun. Its relative pronoun reflects gender/number and its role inside the clause. The conjugated verb goes last.

examples.german: Die Frau, die am Hafen arbeitet, kennt Elise.
examples.english: The woman who works at the harbor knows Elise.

examples.german: Das ist der Brief, den Ada gefunden hat.
examples.english: That is the letter that Ada found.

grammar.title: Reporting processes with the passive
grammar.explanation: Use werden + past participle for an action focused on what happens, rather than who does it. A present passive is wird repariert; a past passive can be wurde repariert.

grammar.title: Reading stories in the simple past
grammar.explanation: Written narratives often use the Präteritum: ging, sah, fand, nahm, sagte. Strong verbs can change their vowel; weak verbs usually add -te.

examples.german: Ada fand einen Brief unter der Uhr.
examples.english: Ada found a letter under the clock.
Lina then went to the harbor.

grammar.title: What had already happened
grammar.explanation: Use the past perfect for an event before another past event: hatte/war + past participle. Make the earlier/later relationship explicit with schon, bevor or nachdem.

examples.german: Der Zug war schon abgefahren, als Otto ankam.
examples.english: The train had already left when Otto arrived.

examples.german: Nachdem Ada den Brief gelesen hatte, rief sie Lina an.
examples.english: After Ada had read the letter, she called Lina.

grammar.title: Although and nevertheless
grammar.explanation: Obwohl introduces a subordinate clause with the verb last. Trotzdem joins a separate main clause with normal second-position verb order.

examples.german: Obwohl es regnet, findet das Fest statt.
examples.english: Although it is raining, the festival takes place.

examples.german: Es regnet. Trotzdem kommen die Gäste.
examples.english: It is raining. Nevertheless the guests come.

grammar.title: Explaining who benefits: damit
grammar.explanation: Use damit for a purpose, especially when the two clauses have different subjects. The verb goes last in the damit clause. Um ... zu usually requires the same subject.

examples.german: Ich spreche langsam, damit alle mich verstehen.
examples.english: I speak slowly so that everyone understands me.

examples.german: Emil öffnet die Tür, damit Lina hineingehen kann.
examples.english: Emil opens the door so that Lina can go inside.

grammar.title: Reporting questions without asking directly
grammar.explanation: An indirect yes/no question starts with ob. An indirect question with wo, wann or warum keeps that word. In both cases the conjugated verb goes last.

examples.german: Ich weiß nicht, ob die Sitzung heute stattfindet.
examples.english: I do not know whether the meeting takes place today.

examples.german: Kannst du mir sagen, wann der Zug abfährt?
examples.english: Can you tell me when the train leaves?

grammar.title: Imagining a different situation
grammar.explanation: For hypothetical situations, use wenn + Konjunktiv II forms such as hätte, wäre, könnte or würde + infinitive. They also let you give tactful advice.

examples.german: Wenn ich mehr Zeit hätte, würde ich helfen.
examples.english: If I had more time, I would help.

examples.german: An deiner Stelle würde ich nachfragen.
examples.english: In your position, I would ask again.

grammar.title: Verbs with a fixed preposition
grammar.explanation: Learn verb, preposition and case as one chunk: warten auf + accusative, teilnehmen an + dative, sich interessieren für + accusative. Da-/wo- compounds usually refer to things.

examples.english: I am waiting for the report.

grammar.title: During, since and until
grammar.explanation: Seit + dative describes a state that began in the past and continues now. Während + genitive describes a duration. Bis indicates an endpoint and often appears with another preposition.

examples.german: Ich wohne seit einem Jahr hier.
examples.english: I have lived here for a year.

examples.german: Während der Sitzung bleibt die Tür offen.
examples.english: The door stays open during the meeting.

grammar.title: Formal written relationships: the genitive
grammar.explanation: The genitive can express belonging: der Name des Dorfes, die Entscheidung der Frau. Masculine/neuter nouns often add -(e)s. This is common in notices and formal writing.

examples.german: Der Name des Dorfes fehlt auf der Karte.
examples.english: The village name is missing from the map.

examples.german: Die Entscheidung der Bewohner ist wichtig.

grammar.title: Organizing a balanced argument
grammar.explanation: Einerseits ... andererseits presents two sides. Zwar ... aber recognizes a point then limits it. Use specific reasons and an explicit conclusion rather than merely adding connectors.

examples.german: Einerseits ist der Weg kürzer, andererseits ist er gefährlicher.
examples.english: On the one hand the route is shorter; on the other it is more dangerous.

examples.german: Die Brücke ist zwar alt, aber sie ist sicher.
examples.english: The bridge is old, but it is safe.

grammar.title: Recognizing forms and word families
grammar.explanation: German changes endings to fit grammar and adds prefixes or suffixes to build related meanings. A printed stem such as besonder or best is a reference notation; use a complete form such as besonderer or am besten in a sentence. Learn the difference between a whole word, its grammatical form, and a building element.
